subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on static charging by electron transfer and electric fields, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain how objects become statically charged for GCSE Physics simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: How can an insulating material such as a polythene rod become electrically charged?
options: By rubbing it with a cloth (friction)
questions.explain: Insulators become charged when rubbed together. Friction causes electrons to be transferred from one material to the other, leaving both with a static charge.

questions.q: When two insulators are rubbed together, what particles are transferred?
questions.explain: Only electrons are transferred. Protons are held tightly in the nucleus and do not move. Electrons move from one material onto the other.

questions.q: A cloth is rubbed on a rod and electrons move from the rod to the cloth. What are the resulting charges?
options: The rod becomes positive and the cloth becomes negative
The rod becomes negative and the cloth becomes positive
questions.explain: The rod loses electrons, so it is left with a positive charge. The cloth gains those electrons, so it becomes negatively charged.

questions.q: An object that has gained extra electrons will have what overall charge?
questions.explain: Electrons carry negative charge. An object that gains extra electrons has more negative charge than positive, so it becomes negatively charged overall.

questions.q: An object becomes positively charged when it:
questions.explain: An object becomes positive by losing electrons. Protons cannot move, so positive charge results from a shortage of electrons, not a gain of protons.

questions.q: Two objects both carry a negative charge. What force acts between them?
questions.explain: Like charges repel. Two negatively charged (or two positively charged) objects push each other apart.

questions.q: A positively charged rod is brought near a negatively charged sphere. What happens?
questions.explain: Opposite charges attract. A positive and a negative object are pulled towards each other.

questions.q: A charged rod attracts a small suspended ball. Which conclusion is definitely correct?
options: The ball must have the opposite charge to the rod
The ball must be positively charged
The ball is either oppositely charged or uncharged (could be induced)
The ball must have the same charge as the rod
questions.explain: Attraction alone is not proof of opposite charge, because a charged object also attracts an uncharged (neutral) conductor by induction. Only repulsion is a definite test of the type of charge.

questions.q: Why can a static charge build up on an insulator but not usually stay on an isolated metal held in your hand?
options: Metals cannot be charged at all
Charge cannot move through an insulator, so it stays put; charge flows away through a conductor
questions.explain: In an insulator, charge cannot flow, so it stays where it is placed. A metal is a conductor, so charge flows away (through your body to earth), preventing a static build-up.

options: A region where a magnet feels a force
A region where gravity is stronger
A region of space where a charged object experiences a force
The region inside an atom's nucleus
questions.explain: An electric field is a region of space in which a charged object experiences a (non-contact) force. Any charged object sets up an electric field around itself.

questions.q: The electric field lines around an isolated positive charge point:
options: radially outwards, away from the charge
questions.explain: Field lines point in the direction of the force on a positive test charge. Around a positive charge they point radially outwards; around a negative charge they point inwards.

questions.q: As you move further away from a charged sphere, the electric field:
questions.explain: The electric field is strongest close to a charged object, where field lines are closest together, and gets weaker with distance as the lines spread out.

questions.q: A spark (a small flash of lightning) can occur when a static charge builds up because:
options: the potential difference becomes large enough for electrons to jump across the air gap
the air becomes a permanent conductor
the charge disappears on its own
questions.explain: As charge builds up, the potential difference between the object and a nearby earthed object grows. When it is large enough, electrons jump across the gap, ionising the air and causing a spark.

questions.q: Why are you more likely to get a static shock from a car after a long dry drive?
options: Water on the road removes the charge
Friction between the car and air builds up static charge, which discharges through you to earth
The engine charges the car deliberately
questions.explain: Friction between the moving car and the air causes charge to build up on the insulated car body. When you touch it, the charge discharges through you to earth, giving a small shock.

questions.q: Why is a static charge dangerous when refuelling an aircraft or tanker?
options: It cools the fuel too much
A spark could ignite the fuel vapour and cause an explosion
questions.explain: Static charge can build up as fuel flows. A spark from discharge could ignite flammable fuel vapour, so the equipment is bonded and earthed to prevent charge building up.

questions.q: In a paint sprayer that uses static electricity, the paint droplets are given the same charge so that they:
options: stick together into one large drop
repel each other and spread out into a fine, even mist
questions.explain: Like-charged paint droplets repel one another, spreading into a fine, even mist. The object being painted is given the opposite charge so the paint is attracted to it, giving even coverage even behind edges.

questions.q: An electrostatic precipitator in a chimney removes smoke particles by:
options: charging the particles so they are attracted to oppositely charged plates
questions.explain: Smoke particles are given a charge and are then attracted to oppositely charged collecting plates, where they stick. This removes them from the waste gases before they leave the chimney.

questions.q: What does 'earthing' a charged conductor do?
options: Provides a path for excess charge to flow safely to the ground, discharging it
Makes it attract more electrons permanently
questions.explain: Earthing connects a charged conductor to the ground by a conductor, giving excess charge a safe path to flow away. This discharges the object and prevents dangerous sparks.

questions.q: A fuel tanker is connected to the ground with a metal wire before its fuel is unloaded. This is done to:
options: allow any static charge to flow safely to earth so no spark forms
speed up the flow of fuel
questions.explain: The earthing wire lets any static charge that builds up flow safely to earth, so the potential difference never becomes large enough to cause a spark that could ignite the fuel.
